title: Psalm 37: Do Not Fret; the Meek Will Inherit the Land
summary: An old man counsels the faithful not to fret or envy when the wicked prosper, because the wicked wither like grass while those who trust the LORD will inherit the land. Across forty verses he repeats the same lesson in many forms: trust, delight, commit, be still, wait, turn from evil and do good, for the LORD upholds the righteous and the future belongs to them.
story: Psalm 36 contrasted the wicked man's self-deception with the abundance of God's house. Psalm 37 takes up the practical problem that contrast raises: what should the faithful do when the wicked seem to be winning? It is a wisdom psalm, closer to the book of Proverbs than to a prayer, and it never addresses God directly. Its central promise, that the meek will inherit the land, looks back to God's promise of the land to Abraham and forward to Jesus' beatitude that the meek will inherit the earth. It sits among the laments of Book I as a steadying word, teaching patience to people who have just been crying for justice.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to David, and verse 25 speaks in the voice of an old man looking back on a long life. Readers who take the heading as authorship place the psalm late in David's reign; others read it as wisdom teaching associated with David's name and shaped in the circles that also produced Proverbs. No particular historical event stands behind it; the situation is the recurring one of the righteous poor watching the wicked grow rich, often by fraud and violence.

The repeated promise about inheriting the land (verses 9, 11, 22, 29, and 34) draws on Israel's history. The land of Canaan had been promised to Abraham (Genesis 12 and 15) and was divided among the tribes as an inheritance under Joshua. Israel's law tried to keep each family's land in the family (the Jubilee laws of Leviticus 25), but powerful people often seized the land of the weak, as the prophets complained (Micah 2:2; Isaiah 5:8). Against that background, the promise that the meek will inherit the land was a promise that God would restore the order he intended.
cultural:
Land in ancient Israel was not simply property but the family's share in God's gift, the basis of its livelihood and its standing in the community. To lose it was to fall into poverty or debt slavery. So the psalm's promise speaks directly to the fears of small farmers and families threatened by the powerful. Borrowing and lending in verses 21 and 26 reflect a village economy in which the poor depended on loans in lean years; the law forbade charging interest to a fellow Israelite in need (Exodus 22:25).

The images come from the land itself. Grass and tender plants in verse 2 spring up after the winter rains and wither quickly in the dry heat. The glory of the fields in verse 20 is the brief spring bloom of wildflowers. The well-rooted native tree of verse 35 is a picture of settled prosperity that looks permanent and isn't. A reader in the eastern Mediterranean would have seen each of these every year.
literary: Psalm 37 is an acrostic, with each new letter of the Hebrew alphabet generally starting a unit of about two verses. The form doesn't produce a tight argument; it produces a series of proverbs circling the same themes, each restating the lesson from a new angle. Key words recur like a refrain: do not fret (verses 1, 7, and 8), inherit the land (five times), the righteous and the wicked, and cut off. The poem is full of contrasts between the fate of the wicked and the future of the righteous, and it is framed by imperatives to the reader: do not fret at the beginning, consider the blameless at the end. The personal note of verses 25 and 35 and 36 (I once was young, I have seen) gives the proverbs the weight of lived experience.

outline.t: Do not fret or envy: the wicked wither
Trust, delight, commit: the LORD will act
Be still and wait; the meek will inherit the land
The schemes of the wicked turned back on them
The little of the righteous and the ruin of the wicked
The LORD upholds the steps of the righteous
Turn from evil and do good; the law in the heart
Wait for the LORD; the flourishing wicked vanish
The future of the upright and the salvation of the LORD

doctrines.note: The psalm teaches wisdom as a long view: measure life not by the next season but by the end. The righteous are those who keep God's law in their hearts and speak justice, and their security lies in the LORD.

Its commands, trust, delight, commit, be still, wait, describe faith as patience under pressure. Faith is not passive, since it does good and turns from evil, but it refuses to fret or seize what God has promised to give.
The inheritance promised to the meek is a future hope. The psalm asks the faithful to live now in light of an outcome not yet seen, the land and the future God has set aside for the upright.

The LORD laughs at the wicked because he sees that their day is coming (verse 13). Judgment is certain even when it is slow, and the psalm encourages the righteous to leave it with God rather than take up anger.

words.note: Charah, to burn or be kindled, used of anger. In the form used in verses 1, 7, and 8 it means to fret or to get heated. The psalm's first command is not to let the success of the wicked set you on fire with resentment, because that anger only leads to harm.

Yarash, to take possession or to inherit. It is the verb used throughout Deuteronomy and Joshua for Israel taking possession of the land. Its fivefold use here turns that national history into a personal promise: those who trust the LORD will possess what he has promised.

Anav, humble or meek. The word describes people who are poor or powerless and who depend on God rather than on force. Meekness here is not weakness of character but the posture of those who wait for God instead of grabbing. Jesus uses this line in the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:5).

Qavah, to wait or hope. In verse 9 those who hope in the LORD inherit the land, and in verse 34 the reader is told to wait for the LORD. The word carries a sense of eager expectation rather than idle waiting, and it appears often in the Psalms and Isaiah (for example Isaiah 40:31).

christ: Jesus' beatitude, Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5), is taken almost directly from verse 11. In Jesus' teaching the promise widens from the land of Canaan to the whole earth renewed, and he himself embodies the meekness the psalm commends: he did not seize power but trusted the Father, and was exalted (Philippians 2:5-11). The New Testament also takes up the psalm's long view. Paul speaks of Abraham's heirs inheriting the world (Romans 4:13), and the Bible ends with a new heaven and a new earth where righteousness dwells. The psalm's counsel to wait patiently while the wicked seem to prosper becomes, in Christ, patience for the day when he returns and sets all things right.

hard.q: Is it true that the righteous are never abandoned and their children never beg for bread?
hard.a: Verse 25 says the speaker has never seen the righteous abandoned or their children begging for bread. Many faithful people have, however, known hunger and poverty, and Scripture itself records it (Lazarus at the rich man's gate in Luke 16, the famine that sent Naomi's family to Moab, the poverty of the Jerusalem believers). Interpreters handle the verse in several ways. Some stress that it is personal testimony, one old man's observation of God's care in his lifetime, not a universal promise. Others read it, like much of Proverbs, as a statement of how God's world generally works, since generosity and honest work tend toward provision in a community that keeps God's law. Still others read it in light of the psalm's whole argument, which looks toward an end when the righteous will be vindicated. Honest readers can hold the verse as a real witness to God's faithfulness without using it to accuse the poor of unrighteousness, a use the rest of Scripture rejects.

questions: Whose success tends to make you fret or envy? What does the psalm say to that feeling?
Verse 4 says to delight yourself in the LORD. How might delighting in God change the desires of your heart, not just fulfill them?
What does it look like to be meek in a world that rewards grasping and self-promotion?
